subject: religious-studies
title: Death and an Afterlife
text: Explain two different beliefs about life after death. In your answer you should refer to Christianity and Islam.
marks:
Award up to 2 marks per belief explained (1 mark for a simple point, 2 for a developed point). If beliefs are not contrasting, maximum 2 marks.
• Some Christians believe in the immortality of the soul – that the soul continues living immediately after death, as shown by Jesus telling the thief on the cross he would be in paradise that day (Luke 23:43) (2)
• Muslims believe that after death the soul enters barzakh, a state of waiting, and will not enter Jannah or Jahannam until the Day of Judgement when all people are resurrected and judged by Allah (2)
Alternatively: Christians may believe in purgatory (Catholic view) vs Muslims who do not have a concept of purgatory – in Islam the soul waits in barzakh instead.

subject: religious-studies
title: Death and an Afterlife
text: Explain two religious beliefs about how belief in an afterlife affects the value of human life. Refer to scripture or sacred writings in your answer.
marks:
Marking: First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks) = up to 6 marks.

Award 1 mark per simple point, 2 marks per developed point (maximum 4), plus 1 mark for a relevant reference to scripture or sacred writing.
• Christians believe life is valuable because it is given by God and is sacred. Belief in heaven motivates Christians to live according to God’s will so they can be rewarded with eternal life (2)
• Muslims believe life is a test from Allah. How they live determines whether they enter Jannah or Jahannam, so they are motivated to follow the Five Pillars and treat others with compassion (2)
• Scripture: “Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in Paradise” (Luke 23:43) – shows Christians that the afterlife begins after death, making earthly life a preparation for eternity (1)
OR: “No soul may die except with God’s permission at a predestined time” (Qur’an 3:145) – shows Muslims that God controls life and death (1)

subject: religious-studies
title: Death and an Afterlife
text: Explain two Muslim beliefs about what happens after death. Refer to scripture or sacred writings in your answer.
marks:
Marking: First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks) = up to 6 marks.

Award 1 mark per simple point, 2 marks per developed point (maximum 4), plus 1 mark for a relevant reference to scripture or sacred writing.
• Muslims believe that after death the soul enters barzakh – a state of waiting between death and the Day of Judgement where angels question the soul about its faith (2)
• On the Day of Judgement, all people will be resurrected and judged by Allah. Those who lived righteously will enter Jannah (paradise) and those who did evil will be sent to Jahannam (hell) (2)
• Scripture: “No soul may die except with God’s permission at a predestined time” (Qur’an 3:145) – shows that Allah controls life and death and has a plan for every person (1)
OR: “Do not kill each other, for God is merciful to you” (Qur’an 4:29) – reinforces the sanctity of life because Allah alone decides when life ends (1)

subject: religious-studies
title: Sin, Salvation & Atonement
text: Explain two Christian beliefs about atonement. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
marks:
Students may include:
• Jesus’s death on the cross restored the relationship between God and humanity. Isaiah 53:5 states: ‘He was pierced for our transgressions… by his wounds we are healed.’ Christians believe Jesus took the punishment humans deserved for their sins, making reconciliation with God possible. (1–2 marks)
• Jesus was a substitute for sinful humanity — he died in our place. Romans 5:8 states: ‘God demonstrates his own love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.’ This shows atonement is an act of God’s love, not something humans earned. (1–2 marks)
• Source named and applied to support each belief. (1–2 marks)
Two beliefs with named sources. [6 marks]

subject: religious-studies
title: Creation, the Afterlife & Judgement
text: Explain two Christian beliefs about creation. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
marks:
Students may include:
• God created the world from nothing. Genesis 1:1–3 states: ‘In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth’ and ‘the Spirit of God was hovering over the waters.’ This shows both God the Father and the Holy Spirit were involved in creation. (1–2 marks)
• The Word (Jesus/the Son) was involved in creation. John 1:1–3 states: ‘Through him all things were made; without him nothing was made that has been made.’ This means Jesus existed before creation and was the agent through whom God created everything. (1–2 marks)
• Source named and applied for additional marks. (1–2 marks)
Two beliefs, each explained and supported by a named source. [6 marks]

subject: religious-studies
title: The Nature of God & the Trinity
text: Explain two Christian beliefs about the nature of God. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
marks:
Students may include:
• God is omnipotent — all-powerful. Supported by Luke 1:37: ‘Nothing is impossible with God.’ This was spoken by the Angel Gabriel to Mary, showing God’s power has no limits. (1–2 marks)
• God is benevolent — all-loving. Supported by John 3:16: ‘God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son.’ Sending Jesus is seen as God’s greatest act of love. (1–2 marks)
• God is just — fair. Supported by 2 Thessalonians 1:6: ‘God is just: He will pay back trouble to those who trouble you.’ (1–2 marks)
• Source named and applied to the belief for additional marks.
Two beliefs, each explained and supported by a source of authority. [6 marks]

subject: religious-studies
title: Akhirah: Life After Death
text: Explain two Muslim beliefs about the Day of Judgement. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Muslim belief and teaching in your answer.
marks:
Marking: First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks) = up to 6 marks.

Belief 1 (2 marks): Muslims believe that on the Day of Judgement, every person who has ever lived will be resurrected from the dead and given a new body. Allah will judge each person based on their recorded deeds.

Belief 2 (2 marks): Muslims believe that the angel Israfil will blow a trumpet to announce the end of the present world and the beginning of judgement. All people will then stand before Allah to account for their actions.

Source of authority (2 marks): The Qur’an states: ‘The record of their deeds will be laid open and you will see the guilty, dismayed at what they contain’ (Qur’an 18:49), which teaches that every deed, small or large, will be accounted for.
[6 marks]

subject: religious-studies
title: Nuclear Weapons and Weapons of Mass Destruction
text: Explain two religious beliefs about nuclear weapons. Refer to scripture or sacred writings in your answer.
marks:
Marking: First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks) = up to 6 marks.

First belief: simple explanation = 1 mark, detailed explanation = 2 marks. Second belief: simple explanation = 1 mark, detailed explanation = 2 marks. Relevant scripture reference = 1 mark.
Students may include:
• Many Christians oppose nuclear weapons because they cause indiscriminate destruction. Jesus taught 'Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God' (Matthew 5:9), meaning Christians should promote peace rather than stockpile weapons that could kill millions.
• Many Muslims believe nuclear weapons are not approved by Allah because the Qur'an teaches that responses to aggression must be proportionate: 'If you have to respond to an attack, make your response proportionate' (Qur'an 16:126). Nuclear weapons cause disproportionate, indiscriminate destruction.
• Some Christians may accept nuclear deterrence to protect innocent lives, applying the principle of 'love your neighbour' (Matthew 22:39) by keeping peace through strength.

subject: religious-studies
title: Nuclear Weapons and Weapons of Mass Destruction
text: Explain two religious teachings about weapons of mass destruction. Refer to scripture or sacred writings in your answer.
marks:
Marking: First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks) = up to 6 marks.

First teaching: simple explanation = 1 mark, detailed explanation = 2 marks. Second teaching: simple explanation = 1 mark, detailed explanation = 2 marks. Relevant scripture reference = 1 mark.
Students may include:
• Christians believe WMD contradict the teaching to 'love your neighbour as yourself' (Matthew 22:39) because they cause indiscriminate suffering to innocent people. Several popes have spoken out against WMD, arguing the money spent could help the poor instead.
• Muslims believe WMD go beyond what is permitted in self-defence. The Qur'an teaches that violence must be proportionate: 'If you have to respond to an attack, make your response proportionate' (Qur'an 16:126). WMD cause disproportionate destruction and harm civilians, which Muhammad explicitly forbade.

subject: religious-studies
title: Zakah and Hajj
text: Explain two reasons why Hajj is important for Muslims. Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
marks:
Reason 1: Hajj is a duty commanded by God — the Qur’an states ‘Pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to God by people who are able to undertake it’ (3:97). Fulfilling this obligation demonstrates complete submission to Allah’s will. (1–2 marks)
Reason 2: Hajj demonstrates the equality and unity of the ummah. All pilgrims wear simple white ihram garments, removing distinctions of wealth and status. More than 1.5 million Muslims from every nation stand together at Arafat, symbolising the Day of Judgement when all will stand equal before God. (1–2 marks)
Source: Muhammad said ‘Hajj is Arafat,’ showing that standing in prayer at Arafat is the most essential part of the pilgrimage. / Qur’an 3:97. (1–2 marks)

subject: religious-studies
title: Festivals and Commemorations
text: Explain two ways in which a Muslim celebrates Eid al-Adha. Refer to scripture or sacred writings in your answer.
marks:
Marking: First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks) = up to 6 marks.

Students may include some of the following points:
• Muslims perform Qurbani — the sacrifice of an animal (usually a sheep or goat). The meat is divided into three parts: one third for the family, one third for friends, and one third for the poor. This recalls Ibrahim’s willingness to sacrifice his son when Allah provided a ram instead.
• Muslims attend special Eid prayers at the mosque and listen to a sermon. They wear their best clothes and exchange gifts with family and friends.
• Reference to sacred writing, e.g. the Qur’an teaches that Ibrahim agreed to sacrifice his son (37:102) / ‘Ibrahim was tempted at three places but Jibril told him to pelt him’ (Hadith) / the story of Ibrahim’s complete submission to Allah.
• For pilgrims on Hajj, men shave their heads and women cut a lock of hair, symbolising the completion of the main pilgrimage rituals.
Award marks for identification, development, and relevant reference to scripture. [6 marks]

subject: religious-studies
title: Festivals and Commemorations
text: Explain two ways in which a Muslim celebrates Eid al-Fitr. Refer to scripture or sacred writings in your answer.
marks:
Marking: First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks) = up to 6 marks.

Students may include some of the following points:
• Muslims give Zakat al-Fitr before the Eid prayer (approximately £2–£5). This charitable donation was encouraged by the Prophet Muhammad and ensures the poor can also celebrate Eid.
• Muslims attend the Eid prayer in the mosque or an open area and listen to a sermon from the Imam. They exchange gifts and share a special meal to signify the end of Ramadan.
• Reference to scripture: ‘He wants that you must complete the same number of days, and that you must magnify Allah for having guided you so that you may be grateful to Him’ (Qur’an 2:185).
• ‘Verily it is only a festival for he whose fast Allah has accepted’ — this Hadith links the celebration directly to the successful completion of Sawm.
• Muslims rise early and bathe, following the Sunnah of the Prophet who bathed on the day of Fitr and Adha (Hadith).
Award marks for identification, development, and relevant reference to scripture. [6 marks]

subject: religious-studies
title: Key Beliefs: Sunni and Shi'a Islam
text: Explain two Muslim beliefs about Usul ad-Din. Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
marks:
First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks):
• Adalat (Divine Justice): Shi'a Muslims believe Allah is perfectly just and never acts unfairly. Humans are accountable because Allah judges everyone fairly. This motivates Shi'a Muslims to pursue justice in their own lives.
• Imamate: Shi'a Muslims believe that twelve divinely appointed Imams from Muhammad's family were the rightful leaders after him. They are infallible and protect the true message of Islam. The twelfth Imam is believed to be in hiding.
• Source: Surah 16:90 — 'Indeed, Allah orders justice and good conduct' — supports the belief that Allah is just and expects justice from believers.
[6 marks]

subject: religious-studies
title: Key Beliefs: Sunni and Shi'a Islam
text:
'There is no real difference between Sunni and Shi'a beliefs.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Muslim teachings
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
marks:
Top band (10–12) Well-argued response with reasoned consideration of different points of view, supported by knowledge and religious references.
Upper-mid band (7–9) Reasoned consideration with clear reference to religion.
Lower-mid band (4–6) Reasoned consideration of a point of view. Maximum 6 marks if there is no reference to religion.
Lower band (1–3) Point of view with reason(s) stated.

Arguments supporting the statement:
• Both traditions share Tawhid — the absolute belief in one God. Surah 112 is central to both.
• Both accept Muhammad as the Seal of the Prophets (Surah 33:40) and follow the Qur'an as the uncorrupted word of Allah.
• Both believe in a Day of Judgement and accountability. Both carry out the same five key duties.

Arguments against:
• Shi'a belief includes Adalat (divine justice) as a separate root, emphasising Allah's fairness in a way the Sunni articles do not.
• The Imamate is a major theological difference — Shi'a Muslims believe in twelve infallible, divinely appointed Imams. Sunni Islam has no equivalent belief.
• Sunni belief lists angels and predestination as separate articles; Shi'a belief does not single them out as core roots.

subject: religious-studies
title: Families, Gender Roles & Equality
text: Explain two contrasting religious beliefs about whether men and women should have equal roles. In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
marks:
Award up to 2 marks per belief (1 for stating, 2 for developing):
• Many Christians believe men and women are equal / Galatians 3:28 says 'there is neither male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus' / the Church of England ordains women as priests and bishops.
• In Islam, men and women have different but complementary roles / the Qur’an (4:34) says 'men are the protectors and maintainers of women' / but both are equal in the eyes of Allah (Qur’an 33:35).
• Accept other valid contrasting beliefs, e.g. Catholic view (no female priests) vs liberal Protestant view.

subject: religious-studies
title: Families, Gender Roles & Equality
text: Explain two similar religious beliefs about the importance of the extended family. In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
marks:
Award up to 2 marks per belief (1 for stating, 2 for developing):
• Christians value the extended family / grandparents and relatives help pass on the faith / Proverbs 17:6 says 'Children’s children are a crown to the aged.'
• Islam places great importance on the extended family / the ummah begins with family ties / the Qur’an teaches Muslims to maintain ties of kinship and care for elderly relatives.
• Both religions see the extended family as providing support, wisdom and continuity of faith.

subject: religious-studies
title: Gender Equality, Prejudice and Discrimination
text:
Explain two religious beliefs about gender equality.
Refer to scripture or sacred writings in your answer.
marks:
Marking: First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks) = up to 6 marks.

Award up to 6 marks:
• One belief: Christians believe men and women are equal in God’s sight because the Bible says “There is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28). This means that in God’s eyes, gender does not determine a person’s worth (up to 3 marks: 1 for belief, 1 for source, 1 for development).
• Second belief: Muslims believe God created all people equal — the Qur’an teaches “People, We created you all from a single man and a single woman” (Qur’an 49:13). This shows that men and women share the same origin and spiritual nature (up to 3 marks: 1 for belief, 1 for source, 1 for development).
Accept other valid beliefs supported by relevant scripture.

subject: religious-studies
title: Gender Equality, Prejudice and Discrimination
text:
Explain two religious beliefs about the roles of men and women.
Refer to scripture or sacred writings in your answer.
marks:
Marking: First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks) = up to 6 marks.

Award up to 6 marks:
• One belief: Some Christians believe that men should lead in the family because St Paul wrote “the husband is the head of the wife just as Christ is the head of the church” (Ephesians 5:23). This means that the man has a responsibility to care for and guide his family, as Christ cares for the Church (up to 3 marks: 1 for belief, 1 for source, 1 for development).
• Second belief: In Islam, the Qur’an teaches that men and women have complementary roles — “People, We created you all from a single man and a single woman” (Qur’an 49:13). This means both are valued equally by God, even if they may take on different responsibilities within the family (up to 3 marks: 1 for belief, 1 for source, 1 for development).
Accept other valid beliefs supported by relevant scripture.

subject: religious-studies
title: Origins of the Universe & Human Life
text: Explain two contrasting religious beliefs about the origin of the universe. In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
marks:
Award up to 2 marks per belief (1 for stating, 2 for developing):
• Literalist Christians believe God created the universe in six 24-hour days exactly as described in Genesis / they reject the Big Bang because it contradicts scripture / some are Young Earth Creationists who believe the universe is 6,000–10,000 years old.
• Non-literalist Christians/Muslims believe the creation accounts are metaphorical / God caused the Big Bang / the Qur’an’s reference to heavens and earth being 'split apart' (21:30) could describe the Big Bang / science explains how, religion explains why.
• Accept other valid contrasting beliefs.

subject: religious-studies
title: Origins of the Universe & Human Life
text: Explain two similar religious beliefs about humans' responsibility for the environment. In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
marks:
Award up to 2 marks per belief (1 for stating, 2 for developing):
• Christians believe in stewardship — they have a God-given duty to care for the earth / Pope Francis’s Laudato Si’ urged protection of 'our common home' / they will be accountable to God.
• Muslims believe humans are khalifah (caretakers) / the Prophet Muhammad forbade wasting water / Muslims will be judged on the Day of Judgement for how they treated the earth.
• Both religions agree that the earth belongs to God and humans have a duty to protect it for future generations.

subject: religious-studies
title: The Environment & Animal Rights
text: Explain two contrasting religious beliefs about animal experimentation. In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
marks:
Award up to 2 marks per belief (1 for stating, 2 for developing):
• Many Christians accept animal experimentation if it saves human lives / humans have dominion over animals (Genesis 1:28) / the Catholic Church teaches it is acceptable 'within reasonable limits' to save human lives.
• Islam generally opposes causing unnecessary harm to animals / Muhammad said anyone who kills a sparrow wrongfully will answer on the Day of Judgement / cosmetic testing on animals is considered haram.
• Alternatively: Some Christians (e.g. Quakers) oppose animal experimentation because stewardship means protecting all creatures / Proverbs 12:10.

subject: religious-studies
title: The Environment & Animal Rights
text: Explain two similar religious beliefs about the importance of protecting the environment. In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
marks:
Award up to 2 marks per belief (1 for stating, 2 for developing):
• Christians believe in stewardship of God’s creation / Genesis 2:15 / Pope Francis called on all people to protect 'our common home' in Laudato Si’.
• Muslims believe humans are khalifah / they are accountable to Allah for how they treat the earth / Muhammad forbade wasting water.
• Both religions teach that the earth belongs to God and humans have a duty to use its resources responsibly for future generations.

subject: religious-studies
title: Relationships, Marriage & Divorce
text: Explain two similar religious beliefs about sex before marriage. In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
marks:
Award up to 2 marks per belief (1 for stating, 2 for developing):
• Christianity teaches sex before marriage is wrong / Catholics cite 1 Corinthians 6:18 'Flee from sexual immorality' / Pope Pius XI stated sex must be within marriage.
• Islam also teaches sex before marriage is forbidden / sex outside marriage is classified as zinah / the Qur’an forbids it and Shari’ah law treats it as a serious offence.
• Both religions agree because they believe sex is sacred and belongs within the commitment of marriage.

subject: religious-studies
title: Relationships, Marriage & Divorce
text: Explain two contrasting religious beliefs about whether cohabitation is acceptable. In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
marks:
Award up to 2 marks per belief (1 for stating, 2 for developing):
• Some liberal Christians accept cohabitation in a committed, loving relationship / they argue that love and faithfulness matter more than a legal ceremony / the Church of England does not condemn cohabiting couples.
• Islam does not accept cohabitation / sexual relationships must only take place within marriage / sex outside marriage is zinah (forbidden) under Shari’ah law.
• Accept other valid contrasting beliefs, e.g. Catholic vs liberal Protestant views.

subject: religious-studies
title: Families and Contemporary Family Issues
text:
Explain two religious beliefs about the role of parents in a family.
Refer to scripture or sacred writings in your answer.
marks:
Marking: First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks) = up to 6 marks.

Award up to 6 marks: 1 mark per simple point, 2 marks per developed point, 1 mark for a relevant reference to scripture. If only one religious belief is mentioned, maximum 2 marks + 1 mark for scriptural reference.
Possible answers:
• Christians believe parents must care for and provide for their families. ‘Anyone who does not provide for their relatives, and especially for their own household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever’ (1 Timothy 5:8). This shows that failing to look after your family goes against the Christian faith (developed point + scripture = 3 marks).
• Muslims believe parents should raise their children in the faith of Islam, teaching them to pray and live a good Muslim life. The Hadith teaches: ‘Honour your children and perfect their manners.’ This shows that parents have a duty to set a moral example (developed point + scripture = 3 marks).

subject: religious-studies
title: Families and Contemporary Family Issues
text:
Explain two religious beliefs about the nature of the family.
Refer to scripture or sacred writings in your answer.
marks:
Marking: First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks) = up to 6 marks.

Award up to 6 marks: 1 mark per simple point, 2 marks per developed point, 1 mark for a relevant reference to scripture. If only one religious belief is mentioned, maximum 2 marks + 1 mark for scriptural reference.
Possible answers:
• Christians believe the family provides the basis for a stable society and reflects the family of God. ‘Children are a heritage from the Lord, offspring a reward from him’ (Psalm 127:3). This shows that having a family is seen as a gift and blessing from God (developed point + scripture = 3 marks).
• In Islam, the extended family is the basis of Islamic society and part of God’s plan for human beings. The Qur’an teaches: ‘Your Lord has commanded that you should worship none but Him, and that you be kind to your parents’ (Qur’an 17:23). This shows the importance of family relationships in Islam (developed point + scripture = 3 marks).

subject: religious-studies
title: Contraception & Same-Sex Relationships
text: Explain two contrasting religious beliefs about contraception. In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
marks:
Award up to 2 marks per belief (1 for stating, 2 for developing):
• The Catholic Church opposes artificial contraception / Humanae Vitae (1968) taught that every sexual act must be open to creating life / only natural family planning is permitted.
• Many Muslim scholars accept contraception within marriage / the Hadith records that companions of the Prophet practised withdrawal and he did not forbid it / contraception is acceptable if pregnancy would harm the mother or the family cannot afford more children.
• Alternatively: Protestant Christians accept artificial contraception / the Methodist Church said 'responsible contraception is a welcome means towards fulfilment in marriage.'

subject: religious-studies
title: Contraception & Same-Sex Relationships
text: Explain two similar religious beliefs about sexual relationships before marriage. In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
marks:
Award up to 2 marks per belief (1 for stating, 2 for developing):
• The Catholic Church teaches that sex before marriage is wrong / 1 Corinthians 6:18 says 'Flee from sexual immorality' / sex should only take place within the commitment of marriage.
• Islam also teaches that sex before marriage is strictly forbidden / the Qur’an prohibits zinah (unlawful sex) / under Shari’ah law, sex outside marriage is a serious offence.
• Both religions agree because they believe sex is sacred and belongs within marriage.

subject: religious-studies
title: Incarnation, Crucifixion & Resurrection
text: Explain two Christian beliefs about the incarnation. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
marks:
Students may include:
• God became human in Jesus Christ. John 1:14 states: ‘The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us.’ The ‘Word’ refers to God the Son, who took on human form to live among people. This shows God’s love for humanity. (1–2 marks)
• Jesus is both fully God and fully human. The Nicene Creed affirms Jesus as ‘God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God.’ He was not half-God or God pretending to be human, but genuinely both. This was necessary for salvation — only someone who was both could bridge the gap between God and humanity. (1–2 marks)
• Source named and applied for additional marks. (1–2 marks)
Two beliefs with named sources of authority. [6 marks]

subject: religious-studies
title: Salah and Sawm
text: Explain two reasons why Sawm during Ramadan is important for Muslims. Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
marks:
Reason 1: Sawm develops taqwa (God-consciousness) and self-discipline. By denying basic physical needs from dawn to sunset, Muslims strengthen their willpower and demonstrate obedience to Allah. This helps them resist temptation throughout the year. (1–2 marks)
Reason 2: Fasting creates empathy with the poor and hungry. By experiencing hunger first-hand, Muslims develop compassion and are motivated to give charity (Zakah). This strengthens social bonds within the ummah. (1–2 marks)
Source: The Qur’an states ‘It was in the month of Ramadan that the Qur’an was revealed as guidance for mankind. So any one of you who is present that month should fast’ (2:185), showing that fasting is a direct command from Allah linked to the revelation of His guidance. (1–2 marks)

subject: religious-studies
title: Mission, Evangelism and World Poverty
text: Explain two different ways Christians can encourage the growth of the Church.
marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each way explained (1 mark for identifying, 1 mark for development). The two ways must be contrasting.
• Some Christians encourage Church growth through personal evangelism — talking to friends, family, and colleagues about their faith and inviting them to church services or events. This is a one-to-one, informal approach.
• In contrast, some Christians encourage Church growth through organised mission work — for example, the Alpha Course provides structured sessions in homes, workplaces, and prisons where people can explore the meaning of life and learn about Christianity. This is a formal, structured approach.
• Other valid contrasts: using social media/technology vs face-to-face preaching; becoming missionaries abroad vs working in local communities; the Church Army (working with marginalised people) vs Fresh Expressions (creative new forms of church).

subject: religious-studies
title: Prophethood and the Holy Books
text: Explain two Muslim beliefs about the authority of the Qur'an. Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
marks:
First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks):
• The Qur'an is the literal word of Allah, unchanged since it was revealed. Muslims believe it was transmitted perfectly through Jibril to Muhammad, word for word. This means it has supreme authority over all other sources of guidance.
• The Qur'an supersedes all previous holy books because Muslims believe those books were altered or corrupted by humans over time. The Qur'an is the final, complete revelation, making it the ultimate source of Shari'ah law.
• Source: Surah 96:1–5 — the first words revealed to Muhammad in the cave on Mount Hira, where Jibril commanded him to 'Read!' This confirms the divine origin of the Qur'an.
[6 marks]

subject: religious-studies
title: Prophethood and the Holy Books
text:
'The Qur'an is the only source of authority a Muslim needs.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Muslim teachings
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
marks:
Top band (10–12) Well-argued response with reasoned consideration of different points of view, supported by knowledge and religious references.
Upper-mid band (7–9) Reasoned consideration with clear reference to religion.
Lower-mid band (4–6) Reasoned consideration of a point of view. Maximum 6 marks if there is no reference to religion.
Lower band (1–3) Point of view with reason(s) stated.

Arguments supporting:
• The Qur'an is the direct, unchanged word of Allah — the only holy book that has not been corrupted. It is the supreme source of authority.
• It covers all aspects of life: worship, morality, law, family and social conduct.
• Surah 6:115 states: 'The word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and in justice' — suggesting the Qur'an is complete.

Arguments against:
• The Hadith and Sunnah are essential for understanding how to apply the Qur'an in practice. The Qur'an commands Muslims to pray but does not detail how — this comes from Muhammad's example.
• Shi'a Muslims also follow the teachings of the Imams, who are considered infallible interpreters of the Qur'an. The Imamate provides ongoing guidance.
• Scholarly consensus (ijma) and analogical reasoning (qiyas) are us

subject: religious-studies
title: The Five Pillars, the Ten Obligatory Acts and Shahadah
text: Explain two ways in which the Shahadah is significant for Muslims. Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
marks:
Way 1: The Shahadah affirms Tawhid — the belief that there is only one God. This is the most important concept in Islam because it means Muslims must worship Allah alone and reject Shirk. It shapes every aspect of daily life and worship. (1–2 marks)
Way 2: The Shahadah is recited throughout a Muslim’s life — whispered at birth, spoken during every prayer, and ideally the last words before death. Sincerely reciting it before witnesses is the only requirement for becoming a Muslim, making it the gateway to the entire faith. (1–2 marks)
Source: The Qur’an states ‘Your God is one God. There is no deity except Him’ (2:163), directly supporting the Tawhid expressed in the Shahadah. / Surah 112 declares that God is ‘the One’ and that ‘no one is comparable to Him.’ (1–2 marks)

subject: religious-studies
title: The Death Penalty
text: Explain two different religious beliefs in contemporary British society about the use of the death penalty.
marks:
Students may include some of the following points, but all other relevant points must be credited:
• Point 1 (Against): Most Christians believe only God has the right to take life. Jesus taught forgiveness, not retribution. He stopped a woman being put to death for adultery in John 8. The Ten Commandments state 'You shall not murder' (Exodus 20:13).
• Point 2 (For): Some Christians / Muslims may support it. The Old Testament teaches 'life for life, eye for eye' (Exodus 21). In Islam, Shari'ah law permits the death penalty for certain serious crimes as a hudud punishment. The Qur'an states 'Do not take life except by right.'

1 mark per simple point, 2 marks per developed point (maximum 4). If the two beliefs are not contrasting, maximum 2 marks.
[4 marks]

subject: religious-studies
title: The Death Penalty
text: Explain two religious beliefs about the use of the death penalty. Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer.
marks:
Marking: First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks) = up to 6 marks.

Students may include some of the following points, but all other relevant points must be credited:
• Belief 1: Many Christians oppose the death penalty because it removes the possibility of repentance and reformation. Only God can take life that he created. The Bible teaches 'I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but rather that they turn from their ways and live' (Ezekiel 33:11). Jesus stopped a woman from being executed for adultery (John 8), showing people should be given the chance to reform.
• Belief 2: Islam's Shari'ah law permits the use of the death penalty as a deterrent. The Qur'an sets retaliation for murder (2:178). However, the next of kin can commute the sentence to imprisonment as an act of mercy upon payment of 'blood money'. 'If anyone is killed unjustly, we have granted the right of retribution to his heir' (Qur'an).

1 mark per simple point, 2 marks per developed point (maximum 4), plus 1 mark for relevant reference to scripture/sacred text.
[6 marks]

subject: religious-studies
title: The Death Penalty
text: Explain two religious beliefs that show that the death penalty should not be supported. Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer.
marks:
Marking: First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks) = up to 6 marks.

Students may include some of the following points, but all other relevant points must be credited:

The Ten Commandments teach 'You shall not murder' (Exodus 20:13). Jesus taught forgiveness and stopped a woman being executed for adultery (John 8), showing reformation is more important than retribution.
• Belief 2: Many modern Muslims believe the death penalty is outdated, inhumane, and not applied fairly. The Muslim Peace Fellowship opposes it. The Qur'an teaches 'whoever saves a life, it will be as if they saved all of humanity' (Surah 5:32). Although Shari'ah law allows it, mercy through blood money is preferred.

1 mark per simple point, 2 marks per developed point (maximum 4), plus 1 mark for relevant reference to scripture/sacred text.
[6 marks]

subject: religious-studies
title: Tawhid, the Nature of Allah and Angels
text: Explain two Muslim beliefs about angels (Malaikah). Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
marks:
First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks):
• Jibril is the most important angel because he revealed the Qur'an to Muhammad over 23 years. Without Jibril, Muslims would not have received Allah's guidance. This makes Jibril the essential link between Allah and humanity.
• Recording angels sit on each person's shoulders and write down every good and bad deed. These records will be presented on the Day of Judgement. This belief influences Muslims to behave morally even when nobody is watching.
• Source: Surah 35:1 — describes angels as 'messengers with two, three, four pairs of wings' — showing they are powerful beings created to serve Allah.
[6 marks]

subject: religious-studies
title: Tawhid, the Nature of Allah and Angels
text:
'Belief in angels is the most important article of faith for Muslims.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Muslim teachings
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
marks:
Top band (10–12) Well-argued response with reasoned consideration of different points of view, supported by knowledge and religious references.
Upper-mid band (7–9) Reasoned consideration with clear reference to religion.
Lower-mid band (4–6) Reasoned consideration of a point of view. Maximum 6 marks if there is no reference to religion.
Lower band (1–3) Point of view with reason(s) stated.

Arguments supporting:
• Without Jibril, the Qur'an would not have been revealed to Muhammad. The entire faith depends on this angelic role.
• Recording angels ensure accountability — they connect belief in God to the Day of Judgement.
• Israfil will announce the Day of Judgement; without angels, key events in Islamic eschatology could not occur.

Arguments against:
• Tawhid (oneness of Allah) is arguably more important because it is the foundation of all other beliefs. Without God, angels would not exist.
• The Shahadah begins with Tawhid, not with angels — this suggests Tawhid takes priority.
• Belief in the afterlife (Akhirah) could be seen as more important because it gives purpose to this life and motivates moral behaviour.
• All six articles work together — no single article is more import

subject: religious-studies
title: Abortion & Euthanasia
text: Explain two contrasting religious beliefs about abortion. In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
marks:
Award up to 2 marks per belief (1 for stating, 2 for developing):
• The Catholic Church teaches that abortion is always wrong / life is sacred from conception / the Catechism states 'Human life must be respected and protected absolutely from the moment of conception' / the only exception is the principle of double effect.
• In Islam, abortion is generally forbidden after ensoulment (120 days) but may be permitted before this if the mother’s life is at risk / the Qur’an says 'Do not kill your children for fear of poverty' (17:31) / most scholars agree the mother’s life takes priority.
• Alternatively: Church of England vs Catholic view — CofE accepts abortion in certain circumstances (rape, mother’s life at risk) while Catholic Church opposes it absolutely.

subject: religious-studies
title: Abortion & Euthanasia
text: Explain two contrasting beliefs in contemporary British society about euthanasia. In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
marks:
Award up to 2 marks per belief (1 for stating, 2 for developing):
• Most Christians believe euthanasia is wrong because life is a gift from God / only God should decide when life ends / Job 1:21 says 'The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away' / palliative care relieves suffering without hastening death.
• Muslims believe only Allah decides the time of death / 'No soul can die except by Allah’s leave' (Qur’an 3:145) / suffering is to be borne patiently because 'Allah does not burden a soul beyond that it can bear' (2:286).
• Contrasting view within Christianity: some Christians apply Jesus’s Golden Rule (Matthew 7:12) and argue that ending extreme suffering is the most loving choice. Humanists argue that a person should be able to choose the time of their own death.

subject: religious-studies
title: Jihad
text: Explain two reasons why Muslims believe greater jihad is more important than lesser jihad. Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
marks:
Reason 1: Greater jihad is a lifelong, continuous struggle that every Muslim faces every day. It includes resisting temptation, studying the Qur’an, performing the Five Pillars, and striving to become a better person. Lesser jihad is only relevant in specific circumstances of conflict. (1–2 marks)
Reason 2: The Prophet Muhammad himself described the inner struggle as the ‘greater’ jihad. When soldiers returned from battle, he told them: ‘You have come from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad — the struggle of a person against their own desires.’ This shows that even the Prophet considered personal spiritual effort more important than military action. (1–2 marks)
Source: The Hadith about returning from lesser to greater jihad / The Qur’an states ‘Fight in God’s cause against those who fight you, but do not overstep the limits’ (2:190), showing lesser jihad is restricted while greater jihad is unlimited in scope. (1–2 marks)

subject: religious-studies
title: Predestination and Human Responsibility
text: Explain two Muslim beliefs about predestination (Al-Qadr). Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
marks:
First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks):
• Muslims believe Allah has complete foreknowledge of everything that will happen. Nothing occurs by chance or accident. An angel records a person's provision, lifespan and deeds before they are born.

subject: religious-studies
title: Predestination and Human Responsibility
text:
'Predestination means no one is really free.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:

marks:

Upper-mid band (7–9) Both sides argued with clear religious teaching.

Arguments supporting:

Arguments against:

• Muslims believe in ikhtiyar, genuine freedom of choice, and Surah 17:15 says no one carries another's sins — which only makes sense if the choices are our own.
• Shi'a Muslims stress Adalat, the justice of Allah: it would be unjust to make someone sin and then punish them for it.

subject: religious-studies-aqa
title: Origins of the Universe & Human Life
text: Explain two contrasting religious beliefs about the origin of the universe. In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
marks:
Award up to 2 marks per belief (1 for stating, 2 for developing):
• Literalist Christians believe God created the universe in six 24-hour days exactly as described in Genesis / they reject the Big Bang because it contradicts scripture / some are Young Earth Creationists who believe the universe is 6,000–10,000 years old.
• Non-literalist Christians/Muslims believe the creation accounts are metaphorical / God caused the Big Bang / the Qur’an’s reference to heavens and earth being 'split apart' (21:30) could describe the Big Bang / science explains how, religion explains why.
• Accept other valid contrasting beliefs.

subject: religious-studies-aqa
title: Origins of the Universe & Human Life
text: Explain two similar religious beliefs about humans' responsibility for the environment. In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
marks:
Award up to 2 marks per belief (1 for stating, 2 for developing):
• Christians believe in stewardship — they have a God-given duty to care for the earth / Pope Francis’s Laudato Si’ urged protection of 'our common home' / they will be accountable to God.
• Muslims believe humans are khalifah (caretakers) / the Prophet Muhammad forbade wasting water / Muslims will be judged on the Day of Judgement for how they treated the earth.
• Both religions agree that the earth belongs to God and humans have a duty to protect it for future generations.

subject: religious-studies-aqa
title: Zakah & Hajj
text: Explain two reasons why Hajj is important for Muslims. Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
marks:
Reason 1: Hajj is a duty commanded by God — the Qur’an states ‘Pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to God by people who are able to undertake it’ (3:97). Fulfilling this obligation demonstrates complete submission to Allah’s will. (1–2 marks)
Reason 2: Hajj demonstrates the equality and unity of the ummah. All pilgrims wear simple white ihram garments, removing distinctions of wealth and status. More than 1.5 million Muslims from every nation stand together at Arafat, symbolising the Day of Judgement when all will stand equal before God. (1–2 marks)
Source: Muhammad said ‘Hajj is Arafat,’ showing that standing in prayer at Arafat is the most essential part of the pilgrimage. / Qur’an 3:97. (1–2 marks)

subject: religious-studies-aqa
title: Families, Gender Roles & Equality
text: Explain two contrasting religious beliefs about whether men and women should have equal roles. In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
marks:
Award up to 2 marks per belief (1 for stating, 2 for developing):
• Many Christians believe men and women are equal / Galatians 3:28 says 'there is neither male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus' / the Church of England ordains women as priests and bishops.
• In Islam, men and women have different but complementary roles / the Qur’an (4:34) says 'men are the protectors and maintainers of women' / but both are equal in the eyes of Allah (Qur’an 33:35).
• Accept other valid contrasting beliefs, e.g. Catholic view (no female priests) vs liberal Protestant view.

subject: religious-studies-aqa
title: Families, Gender Roles & Equality
text: Explain two similar religious beliefs about the importance of the extended family. In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
marks:
Award up to 2 marks per belief (1 for stating, 2 for developing):

• Islam places great importance on the extended family / the ummah begins with family ties / the Qur’an teaches Muslims to maintain ties of kinship and care for elderly relatives.
• Both religions see the extended family as providing support, wisdom and continuity of faith.

subject: religious-studies-aqa
title: The Environment & Animal Rights
text: Explain two contrasting religious beliefs about animal experimentation. In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
marks:

• Islam generally opposes causing unnecessary harm to animals / Muhammad said anyone who kills a sparrow wrongfully will answer on the Day of Judgement / cosmetic testing on animals is considered haram.
• Alternatively: Some Christians (e.g. Quakers) oppose animal experimentation because stewardship means protecting all creatures / Proverbs 12:10.

subject: religious-studies-aqa

marks:

subject: religious-studies-aqa
title: Core Beliefs: Six Articles & Five Roots
text: Explain two Muslim beliefs about Usul ad-Din. Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
marks:
First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks):

• Imamate: Shi'a Muslims believe that twelve divinely appointed Imams from Muhammad's family were the rightful leaders after him. They are infallible and protect the true message of Islam. The twelfth Imam is believed to be in hiding.
• Source: Surah 16:90 — 'Indeed, Allah commands justice, grace, as well as generosity to close relatives' — supports the belief that Allah is just and expects justice from believers.

subject: religious-studies-aqa

marks:
Students may include:

Two beliefs, each explained and supported by a named source. [6 marks]

(1–2 marks)
• Jesus was a substitute for sinful humanity — he died in our place. Romans 5:8 states: ‘God demonstrates his own love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.’ This shows atonement is an act of God’s love, not something humans earned. (1–2 marks)
• Source named and applied to support each belief. (1–2 marks)
Two beliefs with named sources. [6 marks]

subject: religious-studies-aqa
title: Contraception & Same-Sex Relationships
text: Explain two contrasting religious beliefs about contraception. In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
marks:

• Alternatively: Protestant Christians accept artificial contraception / the Methodist Church said 'responsible contraception is a welcome means towards fulfilment in marriage.'

subject: religious-studies-aqa
title: Contraception & Same-Sex Relationships
text: Explain two similar religious beliefs about sexual relationships before marriage. In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
marks:

• The Catholic Church teaches that sex before marriage is wrong / 1 Corinthians 6:18 says 'Flee from sexual immorality' / sex should only take place within the commitment of marriage.
• Islam also teaches that sex before marriage is strictly forbidden / the Qur’an prohibits zinah (unlawful sex) / under Shari’ah law, sex outside marriage is a serious offence.
• Both religions agree because they believe sex is sacred and belongs within marriage.

subject: religious-studies-aqa

subject: religious-studies-aqa
title: Relationships, Marriage & Divorce

subject: religious-studies-aqa
title: Relationships, Marriage & Divorce
text: Explain two contrasting religious beliefs about whether cohabitation is acceptable. In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
marks:

subject: religious-studies-aqa
title: Risalah, Holy Books & Prophethood
text: Explain two Muslim beliefs about the authority of the Qur'an. Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
marks:

subject: religious-studies-aqa
title: Incarnation, Crucifixion & Resurrection
text: Explain two Christian beliefs about the incarnation. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
marks:
Students may include:
• God became human in Jesus Christ. John 1:14 states: ‘The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us.’ The ‘Word’ refers to God the Son, who took on human form to live among people. This shows God’s love for humanity. (1–2 marks)

subject: religious-studies-aqa
title: Salah & Sawm
text: Explain two reasons why Sawm during Ramadan is important for Muslims. Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
marks:
Reason 1: Sawm develops taqwa (God-consciousness) and self-discipline. By denying basic physical needs from dawn to sunset, Muslims strengthen their willpower and demonstrate obedience to Allah. This helps them resist temptation throughout the year. (1–2 marks)
Reason 2: Fasting creates empathy with the poor and hungry. By experiencing hunger first-hand, Muslims develop compassion and are motivated to give charity (Zakah). This strengthens social bonds within the ummah. (1–2 marks)
Source: The Qur’an states ‘It was in the month of Ramadan that the Qur’an was revealed as guidance for mankind. So any one of you who is present that month should fast’ (2:185), showing that fasting is a direct command from Allah linked to the revelation of His guidance. (1–2 marks)

subject: religious-studies-aqa
title: The Nature of God & the Trinity
text: Explain two Christian beliefs about the nature of God. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
marks:
Students may include:
• God is omnipotent — all-powerful. Supported by Luke 1:37: ‘Nothing is impossible with God.’ This was spoken by the Angel Gabriel to Mary, showing God’s power has no limits. (1–2 marks)
• God is benevolent — all-loving. Supported by John 3:16: ‘God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son.’ Sending Jesus is seen as God’s greatest act of love. (1–2 marks)

• Source named and applied to the belief for additional marks.
Two beliefs, each explained and supported by a source of authority. [6 marks]

subject: religious-studies-aqa
title: The Five Pillars, Ten Obligatory Acts & Shahadah
text: Explain two ways in which the Shahadah is significant for Muslims. Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
marks:
Way 1: The Shahadah affirms Tawhid — the belief that there is only one God. This is the most important concept in Islam because it means Muslims must worship Allah alone and reject Shirk. It shapes every aspect of daily life and worship. (1–2 marks)
Way 2: The Shahadah is recited throughout a Muslim’s life — whispered at birth, spoken during every prayer, and ideally the last words before death. Sincerely reciting it before witnesses is the only requirement for becoming a Muslim, making it the gateway to the entire faith. (1–2 marks)
Source: The Qur’an states ‘Your God is one God. There is no deity except Him’ (2:163), directly supporting the Tawhid expressed in the Shahadah. / Surah 112 declares that God is ‘the One’ and that ‘no one is comparable to Him.’ (1–2 marks)

subject: religious-studies-aqa
title: Tawhid, the Nature of Allah & Angels
text: Explain two Muslim beliefs about angels (Malaikah). Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
marks:
First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks):
• Jibril is the most important angel because he revealed the Qur'an to Muhammad over 23 years. Without Jibril, Muslims would not have received Allah's guidance. This makes Jibril the essential link between Allah and humanity.
• Recording angels sit on each person's shoulders and write down every good and bad deed. These records will be presented on the Day of Judgement. This belief influences Muslims to behave morally even when nobody is watching.
• Source: Surah 35:1 — describes angels as 'messengers with two, three, four pairs of wings' — showing they are powerful beings created to serve Allah.
[6 marks]

subject: religious-studies-eduqas
title: The Magisterium, Sacred Art and Catholic Funeral Rites
text: Explain how the Second Vatican Council has influenced Catholic teaching on human dignity and the afterlife.
marks:
Top band: A developed explanation covering: Vatican II (1962–65) produced Gaudium et Spes, which affirmed that death is the moment when the 'riddle of human existence' becomes most acute, and that the resurrection answers it; the council reformed the funeral rite to emphasise resurrection hope; Lumen Gentium re-centred the Church as 'the people of God' sharing in the paschal mystery; post-council encyclicals (Evangelium Vitae 65 on euthanasia, Salvifici Doloris on suffering) continued this development.
Upper-mid band: Two or more clear influences explained with reference to named documents.
Lower-mid band: One influence described without reference to specific documents.
Low band: Brief mention of Vatican II without substance.
